# Robust antiphase oscillations generated by density-dependent dispersal with Beverton–Holt recruitment

## Finding

**Theorem (a dispersal-only source of attracting population cycles).** Consider two patches with identical, compensatory Beverton–Holt recruitment
\[
f(z)=\frac{4z}{1+z},\qquad q=\frac45,
\]
and discrete dynamics on the nonnegative quadrant
\[
F(x,y)=\bigl((q-d(x))f(x)+d(y)f(y),\ d(x)f(x)+(q-d(y))f(y)\bigr).
\]
The fraction \(d(z)\) leaves a patch after recruitment, \(q-d(z)\) remains, and a fixed fraction \(1-q=1/5\) is lost from each patch. There exists an **everywhere nondecreasing, continuously differentiable** emigration function \(d:[0,\infty)\to(0,q)\) for which \(F\) has the locally asymptotically attracting *primitive* period-two orbit
\[
(1,3)\longmapsto(3,1)\longmapsto(1,3).
\]
The homogeneous positive equilibrium \((11/5,11/5)\) is unstable, with transverse eigenvalue \(-13891/8000<-1\). The attracting two-cycle persists under sufficiently small \(C^1\) changes of recruitment and dispersal in neighborhoods of its two points, provided the altered model remains admissible. In contrast, **for every constant** \(d(z)\equiv d_0\in(0,q)\), every nonzero nonnegative initial state converges to \((11/5,11/5)\). Thus migration-density feedback creates attracting antiphase cycles even though recruitment by itself is monotone and globally stabilizing.

In fact, the same exact cycle and its local stability hold for **every** admissible \(C^1\) function satisfying
\[
d(1)=\frac1{20},\qquad d(3)=\frac12,\qquad d'(1)=d'(3)=0,
\]
not only for the explicit interpolation below.

## Assumptions and scope

Define
\[
H(z)=\begin{cases}
0,&0\le z\le1,\\
3v^2-2v^3,\quad v=(z-1)/2,&1<z<3,\\
1,&z\ge3,
\end{cases}\qquad
 d(z)=\frac1{20}+\frac9{20}H(z).
\]
This \(H\) is continuously differentiable (the middle derivative is zero at both junctions), nondecreasing, and takes values in \([0,1]\). Consequently \(1/20\le d(z)\le1/2\) and \(3/10\le q-d(z)\le3/4\), so both retention and outward movement lie strictly between zero and one, with their sum \(q=4/5<1\) for every density. The original source's positive \(C^1\), column-substochastic dispersal assumption is satisfied. The Beverton–Holt map is positive on positive inputs, continuously differentiable, of Kolmogorov form \(f(z)=zg(z)\) with \(g(z)=4/(1+z)\), and bounded above by \(4\).

The result concerns deterministic, simultaneous one-generation updates on exactly two otherwise identical patches, with symmetric density-response rules. It neither claims global attraction to the two-cycle nor applies to every admissible density-dependent migration function. The stability and persistence statements are local in state space and model parameters, respectively.

## Proof

**1. Admissible density response and the exact orbit.** On the interpolation interval write \(v=(z-1)/2\in(0,1)\); then
\[
H'(z)=3v(1-v)\ge0.
\]
This derivative matches the zero derivative of the constant pieces at both endpoints. Thus \(H\in C^1([0,\infty))\). The endpoint values and derivatives are
\[
d(1)=\frac1{20},\quad d(3)=\frac12,\quad d'(1)=d'(3)=0.
\]
As \(f(1)=2\) and \(f(3)=3\), direct substitution gives
\[
F(1,3)=\left(\frac34\cdot2+\frac12\cdot3,\ \frac1{20}\cdot2+\frac3{10}\cdot3\right)=(3,1).
\]
Swap-equivariance of \(F\) gives \(F(3,1)=(1,3)\). The two points differ, so the period is exactly two. This calculation uses only the specified values of \(d(1),d(3)\), and hence applies to the claimed larger class of functions.

**2. Exact two-step stability certificate.** The Jacobian at a general point is
\[
DF(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}
(q-d(x))f'(x)-d'(x)f(x)&d(y)f'(y)+d'(y)f(y)\\
d(x)f'(x)+d'(x)f(x)&(q-d(y))f'(y)-d'(y)f(y)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Using \(f'(z)=4/(1+z)^2\) and the zero endpoint slopes,
\[
J_{13}=DF(1,3)=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/8\\1/20&3/40\end{pmatrix},\quad
J_{31}=DF(3,1)=\begin{pmatrix}3/40&1/20\\1/8&3/4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The derivative of \(F^2\) at \((1,3)\) is exactly
\[
M=J_{31}J_{13}=\begin{pmatrix}47/800&21/1600\\21/160&23/320\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its induced infinity norm is
\[
\|M\|_\infty=\max\left\{\frac{23}{320},\frac{13}{64}\right\}=\frac{13}{64}<1.
\]
Therefore \(F^2\) contracts sufficiently close to \((1,3)\) (choose a sufficiently small neighborhood using continuity of its derivative); successive even iterates converge to \((1,3)\), and odd iterates converge to \((3,1)\). The exact eigenvalues of \(M\) are \((209\pm21\sqrt{41})/3200\), both strictly between zero and one. The certificate requires only the endpoint slopes and applies to every admissible \(d\) in the stated class.

**3. Instability of the positive symmetric equilibrium.** On the diagonal, \(F(z,z)=(qf(z),qf(z))\). The unique positive diagonal fixed point is \(u=qa-1=11/5\), where \(a=4\). For the explicit smoothstep function,
\[
d(u)=\frac{427}{1250},\quad d'(u)=\frac{81}{250},\quad f(u)=\frac{11}{4},\quad f'(u)=\frac{25}{64}.
\]
Because the diagonal Jacobian has equal diagonal entries and equal off-diagonal entries, its symmetric and antisymmetric eigenvalues are
\[
\lambda_{+}=qf'(u)=\frac5{16},\qquad
\lambda_{-}=(q-2d(u))f'(u)-2d'(u)f(u)=-\frac{13891}{8000}.
\]
The antisymmetric eigenvalue is smaller than \(-1\), so the symmetric positive equilibrium is linearly unstable. This instability statement is for the explicit interpolation, not for every admissible \(d\) with matching endpoint data.

**4. Contrast with density-independent dispersal.** Fix any constant \(d_0\in(0,q)\), and define \(h(z)=qf(z)=16z/[5(1+z)]\). For the corresponding constant-dispersal map, because \(f\) is increasing and the two positive weights in each component sum to \(q\),
\[
h(m_t)\le m_{t+1}\le M_{t+1}\le h(M_t),
\]
where \(m_t=\min\{x_t,y_t\}\) and \(M_t=\max\{x_t,y_t\}\). Every nonzero nonnegative state becomes strictly positive after at most one update, since both mixing weights are positive. For any \(z>0\), write \(z_{t+1}=h(z_t)\) and \(w_t=1/z_t\). Then
\[
w_{t+1}=\frac5{16}(w_t+1),
\]
which converges geometrically to \(5/11\), hence \(z_t\to11/5\). Iterating the lower and upper inequalities and applying this scalar convergence squeezes both patch populations to \(11/5\) for every nonzero initial state. Thus no nontrivial attracting periodic orbit is possible under the specified constant-dispersal family.

**5. Robustness.** In the Banach space of local \(C^1\) maps near the two orbit points, consider \(G(F,z)=F^2(z)-z\). At the displayed cycle, \(D_zG=M-I\), which is invertible because \(\|M\|_\infty<1\). The implicit function theorem (or uniform local contraction for \(F^2\)) yields a unique nearby fixed point of the perturbed second iterate under sufficiently small \(C^1\) perturbations. Its first image remains distinct, so it is a genuine period-two orbit; continuity of derivatives preserves both multipliers inside the unit disk. For symmetric perturbed rules, the two orbit points remain exchanged by patch interchange. Therefore the phenomenon holds in a nonempty open neighborhood of admissible model coefficients, not only at one finely tuned interpolation.

## Verification

Run the standalone standard-library script `python verify.py`. It asserts the rational orbit identities, both Jacobians, the exact two-step matrix and its strict norm bound, the symmetric equilibrium and its transverse eigenvalue, the reciprocal-scalar identity, and exact bounds on dispersal over rational test densities. The exact cycle and contraction certificates are rational and do not rely on floating-point simulation. The general statements for infinitely many initial conditions, smoothness, and robustness are established in the proof, rather than by enumerating samples.

## Relationship to prior work

McGrane-Corrigan, Mason and de Andrade Moral introduced the admissible bounded-recruitment, density-dependent, costly-dispersal class and numerically displayed period-two behavior on two patches, primarily using a potentially intrinsically oscillatory Ricker growth law on one patch and Hassell recruitment on the other. Their accessible 2024 preprint does not, in its model definitions, analytical results, examples, or conclusions, establish a stable antiphase two-cycle driven **solely by density-dependent emigration between two identical monotonically increasing Beverton–Holt populations**. Our proof demonstrates such a cycle exactly and proves its local stability with a rational monodromy certificate. The constant-dispersal global convergence comparison is included to isolate the mechanism, not asserted as a new standalone general theorem.

The 2023 study of Beverton–Holt two-patch models with **constant** symmetric dispersal concerns equilibrium population responses rather than density-feedback cycles. Chow, Jang and Yeh (2018) analyze a distinct active/refuge two-patch model; their abstract reports periodic solutions in the setting with an additional Allee effect, whereas it reports global convergence for the Beverton–Holt growth case. A complete full-text implication check of that paper was not possible. Earlier dispersal-linked population results may cover some general mechanisms; no claim is made that density-driven oscillations are wholly unprecedented. The newly isolated fact is the model-class-specific, no-Allee, identical Beverton–Holt exact robust witness.

## Limitations

The emigration profile is a constructed monotone \(C^1\) smoothstep, not a measured field-data curve. The cycle is locally attracting, not proved globally attracting, and the convergence comparison assumes constant and symmetric dispersal with the same positive loss factor. The possible coexistence of other attractors and the precise bifurcation threshold along a family of profiles are not determined. The class-level construction has no empirical parameter calibration. The scientific priority assessment is best knowledge rather than an independence or publication certification; a closely relevant 2018 full text remained inaccessible.
